notice.title: Instance notice
notice.intro: One short message under the header of every signed-in page, such as a maintenance window or “this is a demo”. Write a link inside the sentence as [words](address). It is your own text, so it isn’t translated.
notice.messageHint: Plain text on one line. Link with [words](address): https:// or a single / for a page on this site, up to {links, number} links. {used, number} of {max, number} characters.
notice.toneHint: Warning is for something that needs care, such as data being reset.
notice.shownHint: Turning it off keeps the text, so you can turn it on again.
notice.previewEmpty: Write a message to see it here.
notice.previewHidden: Hidden: nobody sees it until you show it.

errors.message_empty: Write the message before showing the notice.
errors.message_too_long: Use up to {max, number} characters, on one line.
errors.link_label: A link needs its words, up to {label, number} characters: [words](address).
errors.link_address: Use an address that starts with https:// or a single /, with no spaces: [words](address).
errors.too_many_links: Use at most {links, number} links in the message.

passwordChange.askBody: At their next sign-in they must choose their own password before anything else. Their password, sessions and tokens stay as they are.
passwordChange.clearBody: They will no longer be asked to choose a new password. Their password, sessions and tokens stay as they are.
passwordChange.askedDone: They will be asked to choose a new password at their next sign-in.
passwordChange.clearedDone: They will no longer be asked to choose a new password.

users.description: Who can use this instance. Only root creates users; nobody signs up.

create.title: Create user
create.name: Name
create.rootBody: Manage users (other roots included), scopes, settings and the audit log, and approve their own submissions.

oneTime.title: Shown once
oneTime.body: Give this to the user through a trusted channel. It won’t be shown again.

self.title: This is your own account.
self.body: Another root changes your role, disables you or resets your password. Change your password in Account.

userPage.lastSignInHint: A sign-in to the web app, with a password, a provider or a second step. Not rmk or a token.
userPage.dataBody: Everything the instance holds about them in one file: the account, token names, submissions, comments and audit events.
userPage.auditLink: Their events in the audit log
userPage.eraseBody: Erasing ends the account for good. Their email, name, sign-ins and tokens go; the items they published and the audit events stay, under a pseudonym. It can’t be undone.

actions.erasedReason: This account was erased: there’s nothing of theirs to download.
actions.impact: This signs them out everywhere ({sessions, plural, one {# session} other {# sessions}}) and revokes {tokens, plural, one {# access token} other {# access tokens}}. They can’t sign in until you enable them.
actions.enableBody: They can sign in again. Their revoked access tokens stay revoked.
actions.resetBody: This signs them out everywhere and revokes their access tokens.
actions.twoFactorBody: For a lost phone and lost backup codes. This turns off their two-factor sign-in and signs them out everywhere; they sign in with their password alone, and set it up again if it’s required of them.
actions.scimBody: Its next sync sets the account back to what the provider says: change it there too.

makeRoot.title: Make {email} root?
makeRoot.body: They’ll be able to do everything you can, including changing your role or disabling you.

removeRoot.title: Remove root from {email}?
removeRoot.body: They’ll lose user admin, scopes, settings and the audit log on their next request.

erase.title: Erase user
erase.irreversibleBody: Erasing is the end of the account: nothing brings the person back, and the old email is free for a new account at once. To stop someone without erasing, disable them instead.
erase.rootBody: Their role goes with the account.

goes.identity: Their email, name and picture: the account becomes {pseudonym}.
goes.credentials: Their password, identity-provider links and two-factor sign-in.
goes.sessions: Every session, access token and rmk login approval.
goes.scim: Their SCIM links, so the provider’s next create makes a new account.
goes.memberships: Their workspace memberships, open requests to join and open scope moves.
goes.drafts: Their drafts, which only they could see.
goes.ip: Their IP address on every audit event, and their email in any event’s details.

stays.items: The items they published and every version, shown as published by {pseudonym}.
stays.submissions: Their submitted, approved and rejected submissions, and every review comment.
stays.audit: The audit events they appear in, with the pseudonym as who.
stays.workspace: Their personal workspace, renamed, when it holds a published item or a submission; otherwise it’s deleted.

erase.reminder: Nothing of theirs can be read back afterwards: if the person asked for what the instance holds about them, give it to them first. <download>Download their data</download>.
erase.confirm: Type the account’s email to confirm

download.title: Download their data
download.body: The JSON file they would get from their Account page: their account, sessions, token names, workspaces, items, submissions, comments and audit events, with other people’s emails replaced. It counts as their download for the next 10 minutes, and the audit log records that you made it.

scim.title: Provisioning (SCIM)
scim.intro: {name} creates, updates and deprovisions accounts by itself, and keeps workspace roles in step with its groups through this page’s group mappings. Deprovisioning disables an account; it never erases one.
scim.noToken: No token yet: the provider can’t connect.
scim.previous: The token before the last rotation works until <date></date>{hasUsed, select, true { (last used <used></used>)} other {}}.

entra.s1: In Entra, open the enterprise application for Ronne, then Provisioning, and make a new configuration with Bearer authentication.
entra.s2: Paste the base URL above as the Tenant URL and the token as the Secret Token, then Test Connection.
entra.s3: In Attribute mapping, map objectId to externalId (Entra’s default, mailNickname, can be given to someone new).
entra.s4: Assign the users and groups to provision, then start provisioning.

okta.s1: In Okta, open the app for Ronne; on its General tab, edit App Settings and choose SCIM as Provisioning.
okta.s2: On the Provisioning tab, set the SCIM connector base URL to the base URL above, the unique identifier field to userName, the actions Push New Users, Push Profile Updates and Push Groups, and HTTP Header authentication with the token.
okta.s3: Under To App, turn on Create Users, Update User Attributes and Deactivate Users, then push the groups Ronne maps.

generic.s1: In the provider’s SCIM settings, set the base URL above and the token as a Bearer token.
generic.s2: Send the person’s email as userName, and an id that never changes as externalId.
generic.s3: Assign the users and groups to provision; the groups’ names (or ids) are what this page’s group mappings match.

scim.onBody: {name} will create and update accounts, disable them when it deprovisions someone, and give workspace roles through its groups. Its sign-in stops applying the groups claim: SCIM becomes the one source of its groups. Roles its sign-in already gave stay until the provider changes that person’s groups. Next, generate a token for it.
scim.offBody: Every request from {name}’s SCIM is refused at once. Accounts, links and groups stay, and so does the token, for when you turn it on again.
scim.rotateBody: A new token is made and shown once. The current one keeps working for 24 hours, so you can change it at the provider calmly; a token from an earlier rotation stops now.
scim.revokeBody: Every SCIM token of {name} stops working at once, the one before a rotation too. Its requests are refused until you generate a new token and give it to the provider.
scim.newTokenBody: It’s shown once: Ronne keeps only its hash. Paste it into the provider’s SCIM settings.
scim.newTokenPrevious: The token before keeps working until <date></date>, so change it at the provider before then.

usage.policyHint: Counts of installs, removals and runs of the items rmk installed from this instance, by day, item, version and tool. Never who, where, or what was asked.

off.label: Off
off.hint: rmk reports nothing, and this instance refuses usage reports.

choice.label: People choose
choice.hint: rmk reports usage counts unless the person turns it off with rmk telemetry off.

required.label: Required
required.hint: Every rmk that installs from this instance reports usage counts; people can’t turn it off.

usage.minimumHint: 0 shows usage as soon as there’s any. A higher number keeps a few events from looking like a trend, or one team’s habits from showing.

feeds.title: Plugin feeds
feeds.intro: Each tool’s marketplace as it was last built in full: Claude Code reads its own from this website; rmk feed build reads Codex’s and Cursor’s for the git mirror.
feeds.nearTitle: {tool}’s marketplace is near {what, select, both {its limits} size {its size limit} other {its time limit}}.
feeds.sizeBody: Claude Code reads a marketplace of at most 5 MiB from an address. Past it, the marketplace stops loading; add the git mirror (rmk feed build) in Claude Code instead, which has no such limit.
feeds.timeBody: Claude Code waits 10 seconds for a marketplace. It’s built once per change and then answered from memory, so only the first request after a release waits this long.
feeds.notBuilt: Not built yet: it’s built the first time someone reads it.

privacy.title: Retention
privacy.intro: How long this instance keeps what identifies a person’s connection. A purge runs every six hours and clears what is older. Shortening a number clears more at the next run.

ipDays.label: Keep IP addresses for
ipDays.hint: The client addresses kept with audit events, sessions and rmk login approvals, and the email typed in a failed sign-in. Older ones are cleared; the events stay.

sessionsDays.label: Keep expired sessions for
sessionsDays.hint: A session that has expired, and a finished rmk login approval. Older ones are deleted.

feedbackDays.label: Keep handled feedback for
feedbackDays.hint: Feedback people sent from Send feedback that you marked handled, counted from then. Older ones are deleted. New feedback is kept until you handle or delete it.

lastRun.schedulerOff: Scheduled jobs are off (RONNE_JOBS): run rmk-server purge from cron.
lastRun.firstRun: The first run is 5 minutes after the server starts, then every 6 hours.
lastRun.failed: Last run <date></date> failed ({error}). The server’s logs say why; the next run is on schedule.
lastRun.done: Last run <date></date>: cleared {ips, plural, one {# IP address} other {# IP addresses}} and {emails, plural, one {# failed sign-in’s email} other {# failed sign-ins’ emails}}; deleted {sessions, plural, one {# expired session} other {# expired sessions}}, {grants, plural, one {# finished rmk login approval} other {# finished rmk login approvals}} and {feedback, plural, one {# handled feedback message} other {# handled feedback messages}}.

erasures.title: {count, plural, one {An erasure wasn’t completed.} other {# erasures weren’t completed.}}
erasures.body: The server stopped before the audit log was rewritten, so the erased address is still in some events. Retry finishes the rewrite and records the erasure; the retention purge also finishes it on its next run.

page.title: Set up Ronne AI Marketplace
page.notConfigured: This instance isn’t set up yet. It needs a database, its public address and a root account before it can be used.
page.incomplete: This instance’s setup didn’t finish. Pick up where it stopped: the settings are there, the database and the root account may not be.
page.warnTitle: Anyone who can open this page can set the instance up
page.warnBody: Finish it now, before the address is shared.

unavailable.title: The database isn’t answering
unavailable.body: Ronne AI Marketplace is set up to use {database}, but can’t reach it. Check that the server is running and that the settings still match it; to change them, run setup again where it’s installed, or set DATABASE_URL in the environment.

wizard.installHint: Writes the settings, applies the migrations and creates the root account.
wizard.doneTitle: Ronne AI Marketplace is set up
wizard.doneBody: Sign in as {email} to create scopes and invite people.

database.keep: Keep the database already in the settings: {database}
database.sqlite: SQLite: a file on this machine, nothing else to install
database.mysql: MySQL or MariaDB: MySQL 8.4+ or MariaDB 10.11+, already running
database.pickAnswer: SQLite is the default and needs nothing else: one file, backed up by copying it. Pick MySQL, MariaDB or PostgreSQL when you already run one, or expect many people at once.
database.pathDocker: Relative to the app, inside the ronne-data volume. Keep the default unless you know why.
database.pathNpm: In rmk-server’s data folder. Keep the default unless you know why.
database.pathNode: Relative to apps/web. The folder is created if it’s missing.
database.serverOnly: For MySQL, MariaDB or PostgreSQL only.
database.composeBody: docker compose --profile postgres up -d (or mysql) starts one next to Ronne. Use the host postgres (or mysql), the database and user ronne, and the password from RONNE_DB_PASSWORD.
database.name: Database name
database.nameHint: It must exist already; setup doesn’t create databases.

instance.envDocker: Set by RONNE_DOMAIN or PUBLIC_URL in the environment (compose.yaml), which wins over the settings. Change it there, in the .env file next to compose.yaml, then run docker compose up -d.
instance.envOther: Set by PUBLIC_URL in the environment, which wins over the settings. Change it there and restart.
instance.hint: Where people will open Ronne AI Marketplace: the address a reverse proxy serves, or {local} on this machine.
instance.helpAnswer: Links in the app, the address rmk login uses, and the origin sign-in trusts. Behind a reverse proxy, use the public https address.

root.intro: Root can do everything, including creating other users and scopes.
root.helpAnswer: Everything: create scopes and users, review and release items, and override a decision (which is recorded). This is the first root; other people get their own accounts, created by a root, and a root can make them root too.
root.name: Display name
root.passwordHint: 12 to 128 characters. Nothing else is required: length is what matters.

errors.already_set_up: Someone already set this instance up. Sign in.
errors.database_unavailable: The database in the settings isn’t answering, so the setup won’t run: it never changes a configured instance from the browser. Fix the database, or the settings on the server (pnpm run setup, or rmk-server setup), then reload.
errors.public_url_rule: Use an http:// or https:// address.
errors.settings_unwritable: The settings file {path} can’t be written: {reason}.{docker, select, true { In Docker, the data volume is owned by root: run `docker compose run --rm --user root web chown -R 1000:1000 /app/data` once.} other {}}
errors.weak_secret: The AUTH_SECRET already in the settings is shorter than 32 characters. It’s kept, but consider replacing it.
errors.restart_needed: The settings were written, but this process still uses values from its environment. Restart it and reload this page.

users.added: {count, plural, one {# workspace added} other {# workspaces added}}
users.changed: {count, plural, one {# role changed} other {# roles changed}}
users.removed: {count, plural, one {# workspace removed} other {# workspaces removed}}
users.enabled: Enabled. They can sign in again.
users.twoFactorOff: Two-factor sign-in turned off. They’re signed out everywhere.
users.twoFactorNone: They had no two-factor sign-in: nothing changed.
users.erased: Erased. The account is now deleted-user and nothing of theirs can be read back.

workspaces.private: It’s private: only its members and root see its items.
workspaces.public: It’s public: everyone signed in sees its items.
